# Pharmacotherapy for Obesity

## Historical Context and FDA-Approved Agents

The pharmacological treatment of obesity has been punctuated by the withdrawal of agents whose risks outweighed their benefits. Amphetamine derivatives dominated mid-twentieth-century practice, followed by the fenfluramine–phentermine combination withdrawn in 1997 after reports of valvular heart disease. The endocannabinoid receptor antagonist rimonabant was withdrawn globally by 2008 following evidence of severe neuropsychiatric adverse events, including suicidality. The norepinephrine–serotonin reuptake inhibitor sibutramine was removed from markets in 2010 after the Sibutramine Cardiovascular OUTcomes (SCOUT) trial, enrolling 10,742 high-risk patients, demonstrated a significant increase in nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke compared with placebo [@Yanovski2014Longterm]. These withdrawals established a stringent safety framework and reinforced the primacy of cardiovascular outcomes data for new agents, prompting the FDA to require dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trials for all new anti-obesity medications, a policy that has since generated pivotal data redefining the risk–benefit calculus of pharmacological weight management. As of 2024, six agents or combinations hold FDA approval for chronic weight management: orlistat, phentermine/topiramate extended-release, naltrexone/bupropion extended-release, liraglutide 3.0 mg daily, semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly, and tirzepatide 5–15 mg weekly (approved November 2023). The magnitude of pharmacologically achievable weight loss has expanded from approximately 3–4 kg with orlistat to more than 20% of body weight with tirzepatide, a trajectory reflecting deepening mechanistic insight into hypothalamic and peripheral energy regulation. Clinical practice guidelines from the Endocrine Society and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists provide structured frameworks for agent selection based on comorbidities, contraindications, and patient preference [@Apovian2015Pharmacological; @Garvey2016American].

## Older Anti-Obesity Medications

Orlistat (Xenical) 120 mg three times daily acts as a reversible inhibitor of pancreatic lipase, reducing dietary fat absorption by approximately 30%. The landmark XENical in the Prevention of Diabetes in Obese Subjects (XENDOS) trial, reported by @Torgerson2004Xenical in 3,305 obese Swedish adults over four years, demonstrated a 37% relative risk reduction in type 2 diabetes incidence compared with placebo (6.2% versus 9.0%, p = 0.0032), alongside a 2.8 kg incremental weight loss advantage. Gastrointestinal adverse effects—oily spotting, fecal urgency, and fecal incontinence in up to 27% of users—substantially limit long-term adherence, though the absence of systemic absorption and cardiovascular risk makes orlistat suitable when other agents are contraindicated.

The combination of phentermine and topiramate extended-release (Qsymia) exploits complementary mechanisms: catecholaminergic appetite suppression from phentermine and GABAergic satiety enhancement from topiramate. In the pivotal CONQUER trial, @Gadde2011Effects enrolled 2,487 overweight or obese adults with two or more comorbidities and demonstrated weight losses of 7.8% (7.5 mg/46 mg dose) and 9.8% (15 mg/92 mg dose) of baseline body weight versus 1.2% with placebo at 56 weeks (p < 0.001 for both), accompanied by reductions in blood pressure and fasting glucose. Topiramate's teratogenicity—conferring an approximately five-fold elevated risk of oral cleft with first-trimester exposure—necessitates a mandatory REMS program with monthly pregnancy testing in women of childbearing potential.

The fixed-dose combination of naltrexone 32 mg and bupropion 360 mg extended-release (Contrave) engages the hypothalamic melanocortin system: bupropion activates arcuate nucleus pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons, increasing alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, while naltrexone blocks mu-opioid autoinhibitory feedback on POMC neurons to sustain anorectic signaling. The COR-I trial, conducted by @Greenway2010Effect in 1,453 overweight and obese adults, demonstrated 6.1% weight loss versus 1.3% with placebo at 56 weeks (p < 0.001), with 42% versus 17% achieving at least 5% weight loss. The combination carries boxed warnings for neuropsychiatric adverse events and is contraindicated in patients receiving opioid analgesics.

## GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

GLP-1 receptor agonists act on GLP-1 receptors distributed throughout the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, the nucleus tractus solitarius, and vagal afferent neurons to suppress appetite, promote satiety, and delay gastric emptying, while peripheral receptor activation in the pancreas augments glucose-dependent insulin secretion [@Drucker2018Mechanisms; @Holst2007Physiology]. Liraglutide 3.0 mg, administered as a daily subcutaneous injection, was evaluated in the SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial by @PiSunyer2015Randomized, which randomized 3,731 non-diabetic adults to liraglutide or placebo with lifestyle counseling for 56 weeks. The liraglutide group achieved a mean weight loss of 8.0% versus 2.6% with placebo (p < 0.001), with 63.2% versus 27.1% achieving at least 5% weight loss. Nausea occurred in approximately 40% and vomiting in approximately 15% of participants, predominantly during the first eight weeks of dose escalation.

Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly, engineered with an extended half-life enabling greater receptor occupancy than liraglutide, produced transformative results in the STEP program. The STEP 1 trial, reported by @Wilding2021Once in 1,961 non-diabetic adults (mean body weight 105.4 kg), achieved a mean weight loss of 14.9% versus 2.4% with placebo at 68 weeks (p < 0.001), corresponding to an absolute loss of 15.3 kg; 86.4% versus 31.5% achieved at least 5% weight loss, and 50.5% versus 4.9% achieved at least 15% weight loss. In the STEP 2 trial among 1,210 adults with type 2 diabetes, @Davies2021Semaglutide demonstrated 9.6% versus 3.4% weight loss (p < 0.001), with attenuation attributable to impaired incretin responsiveness in established insulin resistance. The STEP 3 trial, reported by @Wadden2021Effect in 611 participants receiving semaglutide as an adjunct to intensive behavioral therapy with a structured low-calorie phase, produced 16.0% versus 5.7% weight loss, establishing the additive value of combined pharmacological and behavioral intervention. A direct head-to-head comparison by @Rubino2021Effect confirmed superiority of semaglutide over liraglutide for body weight reduction. Critically, weight regain after cessation is substantial: the STEP 1 extension reported by @Wilding2022Weight demonstrated recovery of approximately two-thirds of prior weight loss within one year of drug withdrawal, establishing the requirement for indefinite treatment continuation.

The cardiovascular significance of semaglutide 2.4 mg was definitively established by the SELECT trial, reported by @Lincoff2023Semaglutide, which enrolled 17,604 adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity but without diabetes, following them for a median of 3.3 years. Semaglutide produced a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72–0.90, p < 0.001), and this benefit was independent of the degree of weight loss achieved, suggesting direct cardioprotective effects of GLP-1R agonism beyond weight and glucose lowering.

## Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonist: Tirzepatide

Tirzepatide is a synthetic dual agonist at both the GIP receptor and GLP-1R. GIP receptor activation in adipose tissue amplifies lipolysis and reduces lipotoxicity, while synergistic hypothalamic signaling through both receptors confers greater anorectic potency than pure GLP-1R agonism [@Holst2020GIP; @Muller2022Antiobesity]. The SURMOUNT-1 trial, reported by @Jastreboff2022Tirzepatide in 2,539 non-diabetic adults, demonstrated dose-dependent weight losses of 15.0% (5 mg), 19.5% (10 mg), and 20.9% (15 mg) versus 3.1% with placebo at 72 weeks (p < 0.001 for all); 57.9% of the 15 mg group achieved at least 20% weight loss. Nausea was reported by 39.4% of 15 mg participants, predominantly mild to moderate and transient during dose escalation. Among 938 adults with type 2 diabetes in SURMOUNT-2, @Garvey2023Tirzepatide reported weight losses of 12.8%, 14.7%, and 15.7% with tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg, and 15 mg versus 3.3% with placebo (p < 0.001). In SURMOUNT-3, @Wadden2023Tirzepatide demonstrated that tirzepatide following an intensive lifestyle lead-in yielded 18.4% weight loss from randomization versus 2.5% with placebo in 806 participants. Maintenance was examined by @Aronne2024Continued in SURMOUNT-4, where 670 participants completing 36 weeks of open-label tirzepatide (mean −20.9% body weight) were randomized to continue or switch to placebo; continuing tirzepatide produced a further −3.4 kg versus +11.2 kg with placebo switch (p < 0.001), again confirming the need for ongoing treatment. Tirzepatide also demonstrated potent efficacy for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in the SURMOUNT-NASH trial, reported by @Loomba2024Tirzepatide in 190 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and F2–F3 fibrosis; MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening occurred in 62.4% (10 mg) and 79.1% (15 mg) versus 9.7% with placebo, and fibrosis improvement by at least one stage in 35.4% and 44.9% versus 14.9% (p < 0.001 for both).

## Emerging Pharmacotherapy

The investigational pipeline has produced efficacy signals that exceed those of any approved agent. Retatrutide, a triple agonist at GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor, exploits glucagon receptor stimulation to enhance hepatic fatty acid oxidation and thermogenesis in addition to incretin-mediated appetite suppression. In a phase 2 trial reported by @Jastreboff2023Triple enrolling 338 adults over 48 weeks, the 12 mg dose produced a mean body weight reduction of 24.2%—the largest pharmacologically achieved weight loss in a randomized trial as of 2024. Amylin analogue combinations (cagrilintide plus semaglutide, or CagriSema) and anti-ActRII monoclonal antibodies such as bimagrumab, which preferentially reduces fat while preserving lean mass, represent further mechanistic diversification. The broader pipeline reviewed by @Muller2022Antiobesity encompasses FGF21 analogues, mitochondrial uncouplers, and PCSK9-targeted approaches, collectively presaging an era of combination pharmacotherapy targeting multiple energy-regulatory axes simultaneously.

## Practical Considerations

Shared decision-making should integrate patient preferences, cost, insurance coverage, contraindications, and comorbidity profile. Adverse events common to GLP-1R and GIP/GLP-1R agonists—nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea in 40–50% of patients—are predominantly mild to moderate and concentrate during the four to sixteen weeks of dose titration [@WilsonPetruk2023Obesity]. Class-wide contraindications include personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 syndrome. Acute pancreatitis is rare (approximately 0.2%), and cholelithiasis risk is elevated by rapid weight loss. The SELECT cardiovascular outcomes data for semaglutide decisively establish incretin-based agents as having mortality-modifying potential beyond anthropometric benefit [@Lincoff2023Semaglutide]; the ongoing SURMOUNT-MMO trial is expected to provide analogous outcomes data for tirzepatide. Monitoring recommendations include baseline and three- to six-monthly complete blood count, metabolic panel, and HbA1c, with weight assessed every four weeks during titration [@Apovian2015Pharmacological]. Achievement of at least 5% weight loss by twelve to sixteen weeks is the accepted threshold for predicting long-term response; non-responders should be reassessed for adherence, dose adequacy, or escalation to bariatric surgery.
